My paper

Q1. Year 7 Module 1 Listening 1

This task tests the understanding of single lexical items in the context of likes. Pupils write down the correct letter. There are two distractors. Each statement will be heard twice.


Audioscript

1 Moi, les jeux vidéo.

2 J’adore la danse.

3 Les araignées!

4 Moi, le cinéma.

5 J’aime les chiens.

6 Moi, j’adore la musique.


Answers

1 D    2 G    3 A     4 F     5 B     6 E

Q2. Year 7 Module 1 Reading 1

This task tests the understanding of single lexical items in the context of school equipment. Pupils write down the correct percentage. There is one distractor.


Answers

1 13%      2 2%     3 22%     4 5%     5 34%     6 6%

Q3. Year 7 Module 1 Writing 1

This task tests the ability to write single words with support in the context of leisure activities. The first letter of each word is given and the words are supplied in random order.


Answers

1 natation     2 boules     3 gymnastique     4 équitation     5 promenades

Biology

Body systems

Adaptations to environment

Compare similar adaptations in plants and animals that live in similar places.

Correctly use the term: habitat.

Correctly use the terms: community, ecosystem.

Describe some adaptations that plants have to living in extreme environments.

Describe the adaptations of a range of organisms to their habitats.

Explain how particular adaptations limit an organism's distribution and abundance.

Explain some ways in which plants are adapted to reducing water loss in extreme environments.

Identify how animals and plants are adapted to suit their environment in different ways and that adaptation may lead to evolution.

Identify the physical environmental factors that make up the environment in a habitat.

Identify ways in which humans can reduce the effects of environmental change.

Know that animals and plants exist and live in different environments.

Know that living things start from a common ancestor but have evolved to suit the environmental conditions.  

Know that some adaptations to the A1:V2322 in plants or animals can be advantageous if they keep the species alive for long enough to reproduce and pass on their features to a new generation. 

"Recall the term 'environment'. "

"Record the effects of small scale change on living things in a local environment. "

"Understand that environments can be changed in positive ways, e.g. the creation of nature reserves, and in negative ways, e.g. deforestation. "

"Understand that variation in offspring over time can make animals and plants more or less able to survive in particular environments.   "

Antibiotics

Define the term antibiotic (as medicines that inhibit cell processes in bacteria).

Describe the stages of development of new medicines.

Explain why antibiotics are useful for treating bacterial infections (because they do not damage human cell processes).

Explain why antibiotics cannot be used to treat infections by pathogens other than bacteria.

Explain why each stage of the development of a new medicine is needed.

Bacterial cells

Change numbers to and from standard form.

Compare eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells.

Describe how bacteria multiply by binary fission.

Describe how Gram staining works and use results to identify differences between bacteria.

Describe the functions of common parts of bacteria.

Describe why bacteria are classified as being prokaryotic.

Describe, identify and state the basic functions of the parts of a bacterial cell (soft cell wall, flagella, cytoplasm, cell membrane, chromosome).

Explain why bacteria are used to make yoghurt.

Explain why bacteria grow well in certain conditions.

Identify the common parts of bacteria.

"Identify the conditions needed to support the growth of micro-organisms.   "

"Know that germs and bacteria are living organisms called micro-organisms.    "

Recall the conditions under which bacteria grow quickly.

Recall what happens in anaerobic respiration in bacteria.

"Understand that micro-organisms form part of the classification system for living things.    "

Use a statement key to identify different species of bacteria.

Chemistry

Atoms and elements

Atoms, molecules and simple compounds

Calculate the number of moles of particles in a given mass of a certain substance and vice versa. [H]

Calculate the relative atomic mass of an element from the relative masses and abundances of its isotopes. [H]

Describe Dalton's ideas about atoms.

Describe how the atoms of different elements vary.

Describe how the size of an atom compares to the size of its nucleus.

Describe how the subatomic particles are arranged in an atom.

Describe the difference between molecules and giant lattice structures.

Describe the structure of an atom

Explain how atoms of different elements are different.

Explain the difference between an atom and a molecule.

Explain the difference between an atom and an ion.

Explain why all atoms have no overall charge.

Explain why the relative atomic mass of many elements is not a whole number.

Give a simple description of the valency of an element and use these to deduce the formula of compounds (containing two main group elements).

Identify isotopes from information about the structure of atoms.

Interpret formulae to identify the types of and ratio of atoms in a compound.

Name compounds that contain two elements plus oxygen.

Name simple compounds formed from two elements.

Recall Avogadro's law.

Recall that atoms can be joined together by bonds and that bonds affect the shape of a molecule.

Recall the appearance of chlorine, bromine and iodine at room temperature.

Recall the charges and relative masses of the three subatomic particles.

Represent atoms, molecules of elements and simple compounds using a model.

State that all matter is made up of tiny particles called atoms.

State that atoms can be joined up to make molecules or giant lattice structures.

State the approximate size (order or magnitude) of atoms and small molecules.

State the bonding that is found in molecules.

State the meaning of atomic number.

State the meaning of mass number.

State the number of electrons in an atom from its atomic number.

State what is meant by an isotope.

State where most of the mass of an atom is found.

Use a simple (Dalton's) atomic model to describe a compound.

Use a simple (Dalton's) atomic model to describe an element.

Use the idea of atoms to explain why different elements have different physical properties.

Write simple chemical formulae from molecular structures.

Astronomy

Earth and space

Analyse the rotations and axes of other planets to predict annual changes.

Compare different theories for the origin of the Moon.

Describe differences in the seasons in terms of day length and the height of the Sun.

Describe how the Earth, Moon and planets move.

Describe some ways of investigating the planets.

Describe the different bodies that make up the Solar System.

"Describe the movement of the Moon relative to the Earth. "

Describe the positions of the Earth and planets in the Solar System.

"Describe the Sun, Earth and Moon as approximately spherical bodies. "

Explain how we see the Moon.

Explain the changes in day length and height of the sun in terms of the tilt of the Earth's axis.

Explain the effect of the tilt of the Earth's axis on the energy received from the Sun.

"Know that Earth has an axis.   "

Know that Earth has one moon.

Know that the Earth is a planet. 

"Know that the Earth, Sun and Moon are part of the solar system. "

Obtain information from secondary sources to investigate the relationships in astronomical data.

Recall the names and order of the planets in the Solar System.

Recognise the term ‘spherical’.

"Understand that by spinning on its axis, some parts of the Earth are in daylight when other parts are in darkness.   "

"Understand that Earth spins on its axis.   "

Use a model to explain the changes in the seasons.

Use a model to explain the pattern of light and dark at the poles.

Use a model to explain why the height of the Sun at noon and hours of daylight vary with latitude.

Use a model to explain why we have partial and total solar eclipses.

Use a model to explain why we see phases of the Moon.

"Use the idea of the Earth's rotation to explain day and night and the apparent movement of the Sun across the sky. "

Biology

Body systems

Adaptations to environment

Compare similar adaptations in plants and animals that live in similar places.

Correctly use the term: habitat.

Correctly use the terms: community, ecosystem.

Describe some adaptations that plants have to living in extreme environments.

Describe the adaptations of a range of organisms to their habitats.

Explain how particular adaptations limit an organism's distribution and abundance.

Explain some ways in which plants are adapted to reducing water loss in extreme environments.

Identify how animals and plants are adapted to suit their environment in different ways and that adaptation may lead to evolution.

Identify the physical environmental factors that make up the environment in a habitat.

Identify ways in which humans can reduce the effects of environmental change.

Know that animals and plants exist and live in different environments.

Know that living things start from a common ancestor but have evolved to suit the environmental conditions.  

Know that some adaptations to the A1:V2322 in plants or animals can be advantageous if they keep the species alive for long enough to reproduce and pass on their features to a new generation. 

"Recall the term 'environment'. "

"Record the effects of small scale change on living things in a local environment. "

"Understand that environments can be changed in positive ways, e.g. the creation of nature reserves, and in negative ways, e.g. deforestation. "

"Understand that variation in offspring over time can make animals and plants more or less able to survive in particular environments.   "

Antibiotics

Define the term antibiotic (as medicines that inhibit cell processes in bacteria).

Describe the stages of development of new medicines.

Explain why antibiotics are useful for treating bacterial infections (because they do not damage human cell processes).

Explain why antibiotics cannot be used to treat infections by pathogens other than bacteria.

Explain why each stage of the development of a new medicine is needed.

Bacterial cells

Change numbers to and from standard form.

Compare eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells.

Describe how bacteria multiply by binary fission.

Describe how Gram staining works and use results to identify differences between bacteria.

Describe the functions of common parts of bacteria.

Describe why bacteria are classified as being prokaryotic.

Describe, identify and state the basic functions of the parts of a bacterial cell (soft cell wall, flagella, cytoplasm, cell membrane, chromosome).

Explain why bacteria are used to make yoghurt.

Explain why bacteria grow well in certain conditions.

Identify the common parts of bacteria.

"Identify the conditions needed to support the growth of micro-organisms.   "

"Know that germs and bacteria are living organisms called micro-organisms.    "

Recall the conditions under which bacteria grow quickly.

Recall what happens in anaerobic respiration in bacteria.

"Understand that micro-organisms form part of the classification system for living things.    "

Use a statement key to identify different species of bacteria.

Chemistry

Atoms and elements

Atoms, molecules and simple compounds

Calculate the number of moles of particles in a given mass of a certain substance and vice versa. [H]

Calculate the relative atomic mass of an element from the relative masses and abundances of its isotopes. [H]

Describe Dalton's ideas about atoms.

Describe how the atoms of different elements vary.

Describe how the size of an atom compares to the size of its nucleus.

Describe how the subatomic particles are arranged in an atom.

Describe the difference between molecules and giant lattice structures.

Describe the structure of an atom

Explain how atoms of different elements are different.

Explain the difference between an atom and a molecule.

Explain the difference between an atom and an ion.

Explain why all atoms have no overall charge.

Explain why the relative atomic mass of many elements is not a whole number.

Give a simple description of the valency of an element and use these to deduce the formula of compounds (containing two main group elements).

Identify isotopes from information about the structure of atoms.

Interpret formulae to identify the types of and ratio of atoms in a compound.

Name compounds that contain two elements plus oxygen.

Name simple compounds formed from two elements.

Recall Avogadro's law.

Recall that atoms can be joined together by bonds and that bonds affect the shape of a molecule.

Recall the appearance of chlorine, bromine and iodine at room temperature.

Recall the charges and relative masses of the three subatomic particles.

Represent atoms, molecules of elements and simple compounds using a model.

State that all matter is made up of tiny particles called atoms.

State that atoms can be joined up to make molecules or giant lattice structures.

State the approximate size (order or magnitude) of atoms and small molecules.

State the bonding that is found in molecules.

State the meaning of atomic number.

State the meaning of mass number.

State the number of electrons in an atom from its atomic number.

State what is meant by an isotope.

State where most of the mass of an atom is found.

Use a simple (Dalton's) atomic model to describe a compound.

Use a simple (Dalton's) atomic model to describe an element.

Use the idea of atoms to explain why different elements have different physical properties.

Write simple chemical formulae from molecular structures.

Earth and space

Analyse the rotations and axes of other planets to predict annual changes.

Compare different theories for the origin of the Moon.

Describe differences in the seasons in terms of day length and the height of the Sun.

Describe how the Earth, Moon and planets move.

Describe some ways of investigating the planets.

Describe the different bodies that make up the Solar System.

"Describe the movement of the Moon relative to the Earth. "

Describe the positions of the Earth and planets in the Solar System.

"Describe the Sun, Earth and Moon as approximately spherical bodies. "

Explain how we see the Moon.

Explain the changes in day length and height of the sun in terms of the tilt of the Earth's axis.

Explain the effect of the tilt of the Earth's axis on the energy received from the Sun.

"Know that Earth has an axis.   "

Know that Earth has one moon.

Know that the Earth is a planet. 

"Know that the Earth, Sun and Moon are part of the solar system. "

Obtain information from secondary sources to investigate the relationships in astronomical data.

Recall the names and order of the planets in the Solar System.

Recognise the term ‘spherical’.

"Understand that by spinning on its axis, some parts of the Earth are in daylight when other parts are in darkness.   "

"Understand that Earth spins on its axis.   "

Use a model to explain the changes in the seasons.

Use a model to explain the pattern of light and dark at the poles.

Use a model to explain why the height of the Sun at noon and hours of daylight vary with latitude.

Use a model to explain why we have partial and total solar eclipses.

Use a model to explain why we see phases of the Moon.

"Use the idea of the Earth's rotation to explain day and night and the apparent movement of the Sun across the sky. "
